newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECHS PLAN SELLING TOP BANK STAKES TO FOREIGNERS.
newsitem.headline: CZECHS PLAN SELLING TOP BANK STAKES TO FOREIGNERS.

text.p: Key stakes in the Czech banks Komercni Banka a.s. and Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s. (CSOB) are expected to be sold quickly to foreign partners under a finance ministry plan revealed on Thursday.

The ministry said the plan, awaiting final cabinet approval, would be to sell remaining state shares in three of the four largest domestic banks, getting the state completely out of the commercial banking business.
But the embattled centre-right government must survive long enough to put the plan into action.

In a statement, the ministry said that it would first seek a "strategic", which analysts widely believe to mean a "foreign", partner to take stakes in Komercni and CSOB in a process to begin immediately after the cabinet's approval.

"It is expected that (with) both CSOB and Komercni Banka that a method of privatisation will be chosen which will allow for the participation of a strong strategic investor in these banks and which at the same time will bring maximum revenue from the sale of the state shares..." the statement said.
It added that the partner should "provide the banks with the prospect of strengthening of their position on the market."
It also plans for privatisating the largest savings bank, Ceska Sporitelna , in 1998. The ministry did not say what method would be used in the case of Sporitelna.
It said that the Czech National Bank, which has authority over all commercial banks, had agreed with the ministry's plan.

But some analysts think the coalition government, shaken by a currency crisis and plummeting approval ratings ahead of a vote of confidence expected in parliament next week, may not be around long enough to sell the banking shares.

"(The ministry plan) is a positive signal, but I don't know if this will really happen since the question is tied to whether the current coalition remains in power," said equity analyst Petr Posker of Atlantik Financial Markets.

The government, in announcing an austerity package last week aimed at stabilising the teetering economy, acknowledged that its propping up of state-controlled banks had contributed to the lack of efficiency in industry.
Large state-controlled banks have taken measures frequently to help bailout struggling small private banks.

Meanwhile, huge investment funds controlled by the state-controlled banks are blamed for exerting poor management decisions and putting the banks' interests ahead of efficiency and profitability of the holdings they control.
The sale of the state's roughly one-third stake in the third largest bank, Investicni a Postovni Banka a.s. (IPB), through a tender, is expected to be completed soon.

Nomura Intl and Dutch ING Bank NV , have been chosen as finalists in the IPB tender conducted by Salomon Brothers. The Czech government had declared it wanted a "strategic" investor in the IPB tender as well.

The Czech state-run National Property Fund (FNM) holds 49 percent of Komercni Banka, the largest commercial bank, while various Czech state agencies hold a roughly two-thirds stake in CSOB. The remainder is held by Slovak state institutions.
The Czech NPF also holds a 45 percent equity stake in Sporitelna, but 51 percent of the voting rights.
The finance ministry announcement effectively puts to rest a central bank proposal late last year for a "mega-merger" of CSOB and Sporitelna which would have created the largest bank in the region.
